topics.title: Chapter 61 — Putting the System Together
topics.summary: A systems program is correct only when its layers agree. The parser’s length must match the memory operation’s extent. The ownership model must match thread lifetime. The compiler’s numeric assumptions must match the algorithm. The kernel-facing error handling must match the interface. Performance changes must preserve those relationships rather than optimize one layer by violating another. This final chapter develops a bounded concurrent version of the byte-summary utility. It reuses the integer queue from Chapter 49 as an ownership-transfer channel for a fixed set of buffer slots. The program is a batch-processing capstone, not a production service or an asynchronous cancellation framework.

topics.title: 61.1 Data Representation → Machine Instructions
topics.summary: The input is an uninterpreted sequence of bytes. Each byte contributes a value from 0 through 255 to an unsigned 64-bit sum. The count is separately checked against overflow. These representation choices make the required operations explicit and avoid accidental sign extension of char values. Unsigned modular addition is associative, so partial sums can be combined in any worker-completion order. A floating-point reduction or an order-sensitive hash would require a different argument. Choosing a simple additive checksum is what makes the parallel combination straightforward; it is not evidence of cryptographic strength.

topics.title: 61.2 Machine Instructions → Processor Execution
topics.summary: Each worker repeatedly loads valid bytes and updates a private accumulator. The compiler can choose scalar or vector instructions consistent with the source semantics. Independent workers can execute on different cores when scheduling and hardware permit. The program does not assume simultaneous execution. It remains correct if one core interleaves every worker. Parallel hardware affects possible performance, while the ownership and synchronization rules establish correctness across all permitted schedules.

topics.title: 61.3 Processor Execution → Memory Hierarchy
topics.summary: Fixed-size sequential buffers provide spatial locality. Reusing eight slots bounds the payload working set to 32 KiB of byte storage, excluding metadata, stacks, queues, and other runtime state. This is a concrete budget, not a claim that the entire program fits in one cache. Worker-private results reduce shared updates. Adjacent result objects can still share a cache line, so a performance extension might investigate padding or batching result publication. Such changes should follow measurement and preserve the same ownership rules.

topics.title: 61.4 Virtual Memory → Process Isolation
topics.summary: All threads run inside one process and share its virtual address space. Page permissions protect the process from unrelated private mappings, but they do not prevent one worker from accidentally indexing another slot incorrectly. The queue carries validated slot indexes, and the program creates those indexes internally from a fixed bounded range. No untrusted input becomes a pointer or slot identifier. This shows how process isolation and object-level validation work together rather than substitute for one another.

topics.title: 61.5 Processes → Files and I/O
topics.summary: The producer reads from standard input using the descriptor interface. It checks the returned extent and publishes only the bytes actually obtained. Input can come from a file or finite pipeline without changing the processing logic. The example uses blocking input. Queue closure cannot forcibly interrupt a producer already blocked in an external read. A production application needing responsive asynchronous cancellation would integrate readiness waiting and a cancellation event or use another explicitly cancellable I/O design. This limitation is part of the capstone’s stated scope.

topics.title: 61.7 Threads → Shared Memory
topics.summary: The fixed slot array is shared, but access ownership changes over time. A slot is either free, owned by the producer, queued as ready, or owned by one worker. The worker does not read a slot before obtaining its index from the ready queue. This protocol eliminates simultaneous producer writes and worker reads of the same slot.

topics.title: 61.8 Shared Memory → Synchronization
topics.summary: Queue push and pop operations use mutexes and condition variables. The producer’s byte writes occur before publication into the ready queue; the worker’s successful dequeue establishes the visibility needed before reading those bytes. The reverse handoff through the free queue ensures that the producer reuses a slot only after the previous worker has finished with it. No extra atomic flag is needed per slot because the queue handoff supplies the ordering and exclusive ownership relationship.

topics.title: 61.9 Synchronization → Correct Concurrent Programs
topics.summary: Correct synchronization includes completion and failure. Normal EOF closes the ready queue, allowing workers to drain and finish. Failure records an exception and closes both queues so queue waiters can stop. Every created thread is joined before the slots and queue objects are destroyed. The failure flag is only a stop hint; protected exception storage and joins govern access to the actual failure object. A relaxed atomic is sufficient for that hint because it does not publish the slot data or exception contents. Those use separate synchronization relationships.

topics.title: 61.10 Architecture → Performance
topics.summary: The architecture separates one input producer from several compute workers. It can overlap input handling and checksum work, but the checksum is so lightweight that queue and thread overhead may exceed any benefit. A correct concurrent design is not automatically a faster design. Compare against Chapter 60 on representative files and finite streams. Measure end-to-end time, CPU time, and scaling. Varying slot size, slot count, and worker count changes locality, buffering, and synchronization costs; change one parameter at a time and retain the sequential reference result.

topics.summary: The operating system supplies threads, virtual memory, descriptors, scheduling, and I/O. The application adds its own budgets: four workers, eight buffers, and bounded queue capacity. The setup path tracks already-created threads and closes queues before joining them on failure. Resource limits reduce risk but do not eliminate the need to handle unavailable resources.

topics.title: 61.12 Correctness + Performance + Security + Robustness
topics.summary: The capstone combines four requirements. Correctness preserves byte counts, modular sums, and exactly-once ownership transfer. Performance is measured against a sequential baseline. Security keeps untrusted bytes separate from lengths, indexes, and authority. Robustness handles partial reads, setup failures, and cleanup within the stated batch-processing scope. These requirements constrain one another. Removing bounds checks can make a microbenchmark faster while violating the input contract. Unbounded buffering can increase short-term throughput while exhausting memory. A sound systems design treats the requirements as one specification rather than four optional features added in sequence.

topics.title: Worked example — A bounded concurrent byte-summary pipeline
topics.summary: The capstone imports the Chapter 49 queue rather than duplicating its synchronization implementation. Eight slot indexes circulate through a free queue and a ready queue. Each worker owns one private result element, combined only after joining. Companion listing: ch61/pipeline.cpp For ABC\n , the result is bytes=4 sum=208 workers=4 . For 100,000 generated bytes where byte i is i mod 256 , the result is bytes=100000 sum=12742320 workers=4 . The worker assignments can differ between runs while these totals remain fixed. The ownership invariant also explains why returning a slot to the free queue cannot block forever during normal completion. There are exactly eight slot identities. A worker holding one identity implies that at most seven others can already be in the free queue. The return therefore has room, assuming no identity was duplicated or lost. This is a progress proof derived from the resource model, not a timing assumption. On failure, no successful summary is printed. Some work may already have been processed, but the operation reports failure instead of presenting a partial aggregate as complete. The program does not implement a resumable checkpoint, input authentication, cryptographic hashing, or cancellation of a currently blocked external read. Those would be separate extensions with new contracts and tests.

Correct bounds and integer rules establish validity, while cache behavior and compilation determine performance.

topics.summary: Lab 61. Compare sequential and concurrent results on empty input, one byte, exactly 4096 bytes, 4097 bytes, 100,000 bytes, and a larger finite binary fixture. Extend the design in stages: make worker count a bounded validated argument; add per-worker item counts; add a whole-job cancellation policy using nonblocking input and an explicit wakeup source; and replace the additive checksum only after defining an order-correct parallel combination rule for the new algorithm. Review 1. Which queue handoff publishes filled buffer bytes, and which handoff permits reuse? Review 2. Why is the failure flag allowed to use relaxed ordering here while the Chapter 46 publication flag needed release/acquire? Review 3. What additional proof would an order-sensitive hash require?

reading.title: Where the simple approach fails

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Let workers push_back into the shared results vector without a lock, or let main return before collecting workers. The first can race on container internals; the second can leave dangling references.

topics.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
topics.summary: Work items own their strings, so queue operations do not leave borrowed input pointers behind. Main assigns each index once; workers therefore write distinct result elements without resizing the vector. Queue predicates and close are protected by one mutex. Queue capacity bounds queued jobs; it does not bound the already-loaded input vector’s total memory. A streaming input layer would need its own size and backpressure contract.

discussion.question: In plain English, explain why the checks or synchronization in Capstone: bounded concurrent byte processing belong where the solution puts them. Name an assumption that would need a new test if it changed.
discussion.hint: Use one successful case, one rejected or boundary case, and one ownership or state rule. A claim about speed requires measurements, not just a diagram.
discussion.answer: Work items own their strings, so queue operations do not leave borrowed input pointers behind. Main assigns each index once; workers therefore write distinct result elements without resizing the vector. Queue predicates and close are protected by one mutex. Every normal and exceptional path closes the queue and collects workers before local shared state dies. Main prints after collection, so scheduling does not reorder the report. Queue capacity bounds queued jobs; it does not bound the already-loaded input vector’s total memory. A streaming input layer would need its own size and backpressure contract. The maintenance decision follows from this repair: Allocate the result slots before starting workers, assign each slot to one input, and keep all shared objects alive through worker completion. Preserve close-and-collect cleanup if any operation fails.

SLIDE 1: Chapter 61 — Putting the System Together

LECTURE NARRATION
A systems program is correct only when its layers agree. The parser’s length must match the memory operation’s extent. The ownership model must match thread lifetime. The compiler’s numeric assumptions must match the algorithm. The kernel-facing error handling must match the interface. Performance changes must preserve those relationships rather than optimize one layer by violating another. This final chapter develops a bounded concurrent version of the byte-summary utility. It reuses the integer queue from Chapter 49 as an ownership-transfer channel for a fixed set of buffer slots. The program is a batch-processing capstone, not a production service or an asynchronous cancellation framework.

When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. SLIDE 28: Worked example — A bounded concurrent byte-summary pipeline

LECTURE NARRATION
The capstone imports the Chapter 49 queue rather than duplicating its synchronization implementation. Eight slot indexes circulate through a free queue and a ready queue. Each worker owns one private result element, combined only after joining. Companion listing: ch61/pipeline.cpp For ABC\n , the result is bytes=4 sum=208 workers=4 . For 100,000 generated bytes where byte i is i mod 256 , the result is bytes=100000 sum=12742320 workers=4 . The worker assignments can differ between runs while these totals remain fixed. The ownership invariant also explains why returning a slot to the free queue cannot block forever during normal completion. There are exactly eight slot identities. A worker holding one identity implies that at most seven others can already be in the free queue. The return therefore has room, assuming no identity was duplicated or lost.
